justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a view that the underlying asset or indicator is currently trading or sitting near 47.3 and is expected to drift only modestly higher over time, settling around 47.5 at one week and 48.0 at one month. This relatively flat trajectory suggests I was anchoring heavily on recent price or value levels, with a mild upward bias — perhaps reflecting a slight bullish lean from momentum, mean-reversion dynamics, or a modest fundamental tailwind. The one-day estimate is essentially a near-term carry of the current level, the one-week estimate incorporates some expected drift or scheduled catalysts, and the one-month estimate allows for a somewhat larger directional move while still staying close to current levels. In all three cases, the central tendency is conservative, implying I did not expect a dramatic repricing in any direction.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is the natural consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 3 points (45.8 to 48.8), reflecting that short-term moves are relatively constrained by inertia, liquidity, and the absence of major imminent catalysts. At one week, the interval widens to 6 points, incorporating the possibility of scheduled events such as economic data releases, earnings, or policy announcements. At one month, the interval balloons to 14 points (41.0 to 55.0), acknowledging that macro shifts, sentiment changes, and compounding volatility make a wide range of outcomes plausible. The asymmetry here is roughly symmetric around the point estimate, suggesting I did not strongly favor tail risks in either direction.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macro conditions — a surprise inflation print, a central bank policy shock, or a geopolitical escalation — could drive the value well below 41.0 at the monthly horizon. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected catalyst, a short squeeze, or a positive policy surprise could push it well above 55.0. At the shorter horizons, the tighter intervals could be breached by a single large exogenous shock, such as an unexpected earnings release, a regulatory announcement, or a flash crash driven by liquidity conditions. My stated intervals are calibrated to capture 90% of likely outcomes, meaning roughly one in ten realizations should fall outside them even if my model is well-specified — so these tails are real and should not be dismissed.
